full_judgment:
25. On close analysis of the evidence on record, it appears that the case was partly investigated by PW 18, SI Md Giasuddin and after his transfer the case diary was handed over to Inspector Abdul Haque on 24-10-1991. Since then he investigated the case and submitted the charge sheet on 30- 3-1992. It appears from the record that Inspector Abdul Haque had arrested the accused Sadeque alias Sadequr Rahman on 3-11-1991, had forwarded the accused to the Magistrate on 6-11-1991 and on the same day an order of police remand was passed by the Magistrate, First Class. On 11-11-1991 the accused made confession which was recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by MrMd Sahadat Hossain, Magistrate, First Class. It further appears to us that the appellant Sadeq alias Sadequr Rahman was kept in Thana Hazat for 3 (three) days without any order from the competent Court. The police officer therein Inspector Abdul Haque was solely responsibly for such explanation for keeping the accused in Thana Hazat for 3(three) days but he was not examined by the prosecution and without any explanation, as such, the right of the defence to cross examine him was denied and, in our view, such non examination of the investigation officer seriously prejudiced the defence. In this regard, reliance can be placed in the case of Ismail Munshi vs State reported in 33 DLR 5. Similar view was taken in the case of Sukur Hossain vs State reported in 55 DLR 396, Munsurul Haq vs State reported in 1 BLC 421. It further appears to us that the learned Magistrate who recorded the confession was not examined by the prosecution and on the date of delivery of the judgment i.e. on 22-9-1999, the learned Judge of the trial Court merely marked the said confession as Exhibit 7 but none of the witnesses tendered the said confession into evidence so the learned Judge of the trial Court acted illegally in admitting the confession in evidence. Even though section 80 of the Evidence Act provides for making certain presumption in respect of a confession of an accused produced before a Court taken in accordance with law and purporting to be signed by a Magistrate. We are of the view that, having regard to the aforesaid facts noticed by the learned Judges it was at least injudicious to rely upon such confession without calling the Magistrate as witness. The Court is required to see not only that the forms under sections 164 and 364 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was complied with but also whether the substance underneath the law was equally adhered to. There must not be any reason of doubt as to the truth of the statements, be it circumstantial or proved otherwise. In the circumstances of the particular case, it is difficult to deny the accused an opportunity to cross-examine the Magistrate who allegedly recorded the statements. In this regard, reliance can be placed in the case of Babul @ Abdul Majid Khan vs State reported in 42 DLR (AD) 186. Similar view was taken in the case of Senu Mia vs State reported in 3 BLC 441. 

 26. Moreover the confession of the accused Sadek alias Sadequr Rahman forms the only piece of incriminating evidence against him, but his attention to such confession was not drawn when he was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. So, in our view, the incriminating evidence or circumstances sought to be proved by the prosecution must be put to the accused during examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Otherwise it would cause miscarriage of justice as appellant's attention having not been drawn to his confession while examining him under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the same cannot be used against him. In this regard, reliance can be placed in the case of Angur vs State reported in 41 DLR 66. Similar view was taken in the case of Abu Taher vs State reported in 1991 BLD (AD) 80, State vs Manu Mia reported in 54 DLR (AD) 60 and Abul Hossain vs State reported in 46 DLR 77.
